column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent; whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest.” Agreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim).

Lā yuʾminu (“does not believe”): [with] complete faith. Al-yawm al-ākhir (“the Last Day”): the Day of Resurrection. Fa-l-yaqul (“let him speak”): the lām is the lām of command. Khayran (“good”): a word that comprises all acts of obedience. Aw li-yaṣmut (“or remain silent”):

or keep quiet. “Let him honour his neighbour”: the one next to him at home, at work or elsewhere. Al-ḍayf (“the guest”): one who stays with him as a guest. Fa-l-yukrimhu (“let him honour him”): let him be a good host to him.
A warning against the faults of the tongue: a person should speak only of what brings religious or worldly benefit.
Encouragement to be kind to the neighbour in every way that benefits him, and to keep harm away from him.
The command to honour the guest, because honouring him is among the manners of Islam and the character of the prophets and the righteous.
These qualities are among the branches of faith and among the most exalted manners.
The hadith is evidence that deeds are included in what is named faith.
A person should adopt virtuous character in all his affairs, whatever they may be.
Silence is better than permissible speech.
Whoever wrongs his neighbour, does not honour his guest, or speaks much of what has no good in it is deficient in faith.
This hadith guides us to noble character and exalted manners: every believer, when he wants to speak, should think about what he wants to say; if there is good in it for him, he says it,

and otherwise he refrains from speaking, because all the speech of the son of Ādam counts against him, not for him, except the remembrance of Allah, commanding what is right, forbidding what is wrong, or other things aimed at the religion or at keeping one's affairs in order.

He also commands us to honour the neighbour, because in that is the fulfilment of the neighbour's right and noble character, which calls to every good and repels every evil; and to honour the guest, because honouring him is among the manners of Islam and the character of the prophets and the righteous.
Guard your tongue, O man; / let it not bite you, for it is a serpent.
Another poet:
The silent one who holds his tongue has truly succeeded; / his speech may be counted as nourishment.
The second verse is garbled in the edition; its rendering is approximate.
Another poet:
When a man arrives at your home seeking / your hospitality, the roads having cast him upon you,
be smiling and cheerful to his face, / and say: Welcome, be at home, and a blessed day!
Hasten to offer him what hospitality you can, / and do not be miserly with what is bound to perish.
Another poet:
Nothing lasts, so be a story / of fine remembrance, for this world is but a story.
